Neonatal Zebra sharks emerge from their egg cases after an incubation period that lasts approximately five to six months, during which the developing embryo relies entirely on the yolk reserve contained within the large, leathery capsule. Upon hatching, the pups already exhibit the characteristic dark-brown body coloration with pale vertical bars, a pattern that provides effective camouflage among reef crevices and rubble substrates. Field surveys and captive breeding programs have recorded a total length at birth of 28.7 cm [Lb = 28.7 cm], a value that is relatively modest for an orectolobiform of this adult body size. The weight at birth averages 90 grams [Wwb = 90 grams], although documented values in aquaria commonly span a range from 50 to 130 grams, reflecting variation in maternal investment, egg size, and incubation temperature. This initial mass is accompanied by the near-complete resorption of the external yolk sac, and the onset of exogenous feeding typically begins within days of emergence, as the juvenile sharks initiate active foraging on small benthic crustaceans and polychaetes in shallow, sandy habitats. The combination of a well-developed neonate and an early shift to independent prey capture places the Zebra shark among elasmobranchs with a relatively precocial early life history, a pattern that reduces vulnerability to predation during the critical juvenile stage. This relatively large size at birth compared to many oviparous elasmobranchs likely reduces early mortality and may be tied to the extended incubation period in the egg case, a developmental strategy that prioritizes a degree of self-sufficiency upon emergence.

The growth trajectory of Stegostoma fasciatum leads to a moderate to large adult body size, with females typically attaining an ultimate total length around 300 cm [Li = around 300 cm]. A subset of individuals, however, grow considerably larger, and the maximum length reported in the scientific literature reaches 354 cm [Li = 354 cm], a record that places this species among the larger representatives of the family Stegostomatidae. Male body mass follows an asymptotic growth curve, and the ultimate wet weight achieved by males has been calculated at approximately 220,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 220,000 grams], an estimate derived from scaling relationships linking length at puberty, weight at puberty, and asymptotic length in this species. Such a substantial adult mass, exceeding 200 kilograms in larger males, is consistent with the robust body plan of a benthic shark that spends considerable time resting on the substrate. The transition from juvenile to adult dimensions involves a gradual shift in dietary composition, with larger individuals consuming a broader array of prey including molluscs, small fishes, and sea snakes, a trophic expansion that fuels the prolonged somatic growth characteristic of this long-lived elasmobranch. Captive growth studies suggest that juveniles add roughly 15 to 20 centimeters per year during the first few years of life, gradually decelerating as they approach the asymptotic length, a pattern consistent with the indeterminate growth trajectory of many elasmobranchs. The massive size attained by older males also correlates with a diet broad enough to include small rays and cephalopods, reflecting the niche expansion typical of apex mesopredators in reef ecosystems.

When maintained under controlled captive conditions at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the timing and size at sexual maturity in the Zebra shark follow a predictable pattern. Gonadal maturation and the attainment of reproductive competence occur approximately 6 years after birth [tp = approximately 6 years after birth], a duration that reflects the substantial investment in somatic growth required before reproductive effort can be initiated at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. At this stage, females have reached a total length of 213 cm [Lp = 213 cm], while males achieve puberty at a slightly smaller average size of 208 cm [Lp = 208 cm]. Body mass at puberty also differs between the sexes, with females weighing on average 47,900 grams [Wwp = on average 47,900 grams] and males reaching reproductive maturity at a leaner 33,900 grams [Wwp = 33,900 grams]. This sexual dimorphism in size at maturity is relatively modest compared to many other elasmobranch lineages, and likely relates to the absence of aggressive male–male competition for mates and the predominance of a reproductive strategy centered on repeated courtship encounters across a protracted breeding season. Field observations indicate that individuals from warmer latitudes might reach maturity at a slightly earlier age, whereas those in cooler waters exhibit prolonged juvenile phases, underscoring the plastic nature of elasmobranch life-history scheduling under thermal variation. Such thermal sensitivity in development rates has been documented in several captive elasmobranch populations and may have implications for predicting responses to ocean warming.

At a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], as maintained in many public aquaria, the reproductive output of female Zebra sharks can be substantial. The maximum annual rate of egg production recorded under these conditions reaches approximately 100 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 100 eggs per year], a figure that is roughly double the more commonly observed output of 20 to 50 eggs per year reported from most captive colonies. This reproductive potential depends on sustained high-quality nutrition and the absence of physiological stressors, and individual females are known to produce successive egg cases at intervals of several days over a breeding cycle that can extend for months. Each egg case is deposited on the substrate and receives no further parental care, a reproductive mode that, combined with the high fecundity, compensates for the low neonatal survival typical of elasmobranchs. The long-term persistence of reproductively active adults is made possible by an extended natural lifespan; under the same captive conditions, the maximum documented longevity for the species attains 33 years [am = 33 years] at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This life expectancy, spanning more than three decades, is consistent with a slow life-history strategy dominated by iteroparous reproduction, late maturity, and considerable adult survival, a suite of traits that buffers population dynamics against short-term environmental fluctuations.

The large asymptotic size and impressive maximum length of the Zebra shark carry important ecological implications for its role in Indo-Pacific reef systems. Attaining a length of up to 354 cm [Li = up to 354 cm], this species functions as a mesopredator capable of exerting top-down regulation on populations of crustaceans, molluscs, and small teleosts that inhabit shallow, warm-water coastal environments. The elongated, flexible body and broad sensory adaptations, including well-developed olfactory and electrosensory capabilities, facilitate foraging within narrow crevices and under coral overhangs that are inaccessible to bulkier sympatric sharks such as the nurse shark. Despite its size, Stegostoma fasciatum poses little threat to humans and has become a charismatic ambassador for elasmobranch conservation in many public aquaria, where its distinctive juvenile pigmentation and docile demeanour attract public interest and support for broader marine protection initiatives. The species’ vulnerability to habitat degradation and incidental capture in artisanal fisheries throughout its range underscores the need for continued monitoring of population trends and the enforcement of marine protected area networks. The species ranges across the tropical Indo-West Pacific, from South Africa to Japan, and is frequently encountered on coral reefs and sandy flats at depths of up to 62 meters. Habitat destruction from coastal development and overfishing has led to local population declines, prompting its classification as a species of conservation concern in parts of its range.
